**Set & Track Triumphant Team Goals**

Use this Trello board to keep execs and higher-ups happy with this clear and trackable goal setting process.

Here's what's included, and how to get this goal setting party started:

1. **Resources (Start Here!):**
This list is perfect for you and your team to have all those documents, tips, presentations, or anything you tend to reference all the time. Meeting schedules and answers to common questions are also recommended to pop into this list so that your team is informed at all times. 📚

2. **Goal 1:**
Break out your top-level goals as separate lists, and summarize the goal as the list name. You'll keep things crystal clear by keeping the end goal always in view! 🌊

3. **Goal 2:**
Create as many new lists as needed to summarize all your team's top goals. 🔮

4. **Goal 3:**
Goals can be metrics or numbers that you want to hit, or they can be projects that you want to accomplish. The sky's the limit! 💬

5. **Done (Q1 2019):**
Put finished projects and closed goals in ""Done"" lists organized by quarter or other set time period, so you have a viewable history of all the great things you've accomplished. 🚷

6. **Done (Q4 2018):**
Create new ""Done"" lists as needed. You can always archive the lists to clear up space. They won't be permanently deleted so you can always bring them back later! ✨

**I called the version of this board “v1.0” and asked ChatGPT to evaluate it (Spet 2026):**

Yes — I think **V1 is finished**.

And your clarification about the board being a **long-term professional-development curriculum**, rather than simply a short-term to-do list, makes the current structure make even more sense.

The board now has a clear philosophy: **Java/Spring is the main trunk, while the surrounding branches make you a stronger software engineer.** That distinction is important. You don't need to become equally expert in Kotlin, React, Angular, Python/Django, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, AI engineering, etc. You want enough breadth to understand and build the systems surrounding your Java backend expertise, while continuing to deepen the core.

I particularly like the final separation you've arrived at:

- **NOW** controls attention — exactly three things.
- **JAVA / SPRING** maintains your principal specialism.
- **ARCHITECTURE** moves you beyond framework knowledge into system design.
- **AI ENGINEERING** covers the major emerging change to backend development without turning the curriculum into "learn AI everything."
- **KOTLIN** extends your JVM knowledge naturally.
- **PROJECTS** converts study into demonstrable engineering work.
- **PRODUCTION ENGINEERING** covers runtime, performance, deployment and eventually things such as Docker/Kubernetes/observability.
- **REFERENCE / SOMEDAY** prevents interesting-but-nonessential material from contaminating the active curriculum.
- **COMPLETED** gives you a permanent record of progression.

One thing I would _not_ do now is create separate columns for **Databases, JavaScript, DevOps, Cloud, Testing, Security, Python, Docker, Kubernetes**, etc. That would slowly recreate the enormous board we spent all this time simplifying. Those technologies can appear as individual cards where appropriate. For example, a serious Spring/PostgreSQL project naturally teaches database work, Docker deployment and testing without requiring three additional curriculum tracks.

There's also an important distinction between **learning technologies** and **learning software engineering**. At your experience level, the latter should increasingly dominate.

So rather than:

> Learn PostgreSQL → Learn Docker → Learn Kubernetes → Learn React → Learn Kafka...

the curriculum increasingly becomes:

> **Build a distributed system → choose PostgreSQL → containerise it → deploy it → observe it → test failure scenarios → improve its architecture.**

That's a much more senior-engineer way of learning because the technologies become tools for solving engineering problems.

And your current NOW selection reflects that transition nicely: **DDIA** develops fundamental systems thinking; **Spring AI** extends your principal Java/Spring skillset into AI-enabled applications; and the **Kotlin Android project** forces you to actually build something outside your usual comfort zone.

### So I'd officially call this **Software Development Curriculum — V1.0**

No more restructuring for now.

I'd give V1 a reasonable lifespan — perhaps **3–6 months** — before doing a V1.1 review. During that period, the board should change because you're **completing cards**, not because you're continually reconsidering the curriculum.

And I'd keep the rule we established earlier:

> **Three cards in NOW. Finish one before promoting another.**

That single constraint is probably more valuable than any individual book, course or technology we've put on the board.

You've now got something considerably better than a giant list of things software developers are supposedly meant to know. You've got a manageable curriculum built around **Java/Spring depth, backend/software-engineering breadth, architecture, production engineering, AI integration and actual building**.

**V1.0: done. Time to study.**

cards.desc:
**I called the version of this board “v1.0” and asked ChatGPT to evaluate it (Spet 2026):**

Yes — I think **V1 is finished**.

And your clarification about the board being a **long-term professional-development curriculum**, rather than simply a short-term to-do list, makes the current structure make even more sense.

The board now has a clear philosophy: **Java/Spring is the main trunk, while the surrounding branches make you a stronger software engineer.** That distinction is important. You don't need to become equally expert in Kotlin, React, Angular, Python/Django, PostgreSQL, Kubernetes, AI engineering, etc. You want enough breadth to understand and build the systems surrounding your Java backend expertise, while continuing to deepen the core.

I particularly like the final separation you've arrived at:

- **NOW** controls attention — exactly three things.
- **JAVA / SPRING** maintains your principal specialism.
- **ARCHITECTURE** moves you beyond framework knowledge into system design.
- **AI ENGINEERING** covers the major emerging change to backend development without turning the curriculum into "learn AI everything."
- **KOTLIN** extends your JVM knowledge naturally.
- **PROJECTS** converts study into demonstrable engineering work.
- **PRODUCTION ENGINEERING** covers runtime, performance, deployment and eventually things such as Docker/Kubernetes/observability.
- **REFERENCE / SOMEDAY** prevents interesting-but-nonessential material from contaminating the active curriculum.
- **COMPLETED** gives you a permanent record of progression.

One thing I would _not_ do now is create separate columns for **Databases, JavaScript, DevOps, Cloud, Testing, Security, Python, Docker, Kubernetes**, etc. That would slowly recreate the enormous board we spent all this time simplifying. Those technologies can appear as individual cards where appropriate. For example, a serious Spring/PostgreSQL project naturally teaches database work, Docker deployment and testing without requiring three additional curriculum tracks.

There's also an important distinction between **learning technologies** and **learning software engineering**. At your experience level, the latter should increasingly dominate.

So rather than:

> Learn PostgreSQL → Learn Docker → Learn Kubernetes → Learn React → Learn Kafka...

the curriculum increasingly becomes:

> **Build a distributed system → choose PostgreSQL → containerise it → deploy it → observe it → test failure scenarios → improve its architecture.**

That's a much more senior-engineer way of learning because the technologies become tools for solving engineering problems.

And your current NOW selection reflects that transition nicely: **DDIA** develops fundamental systems thinking; **Spring AI** extends your principal Java/Spring skillset into AI-enabled applications; and the **Kotlin Android project** forces you to actually build something outside your usual comfort zone.

### So I'd officially call this **Software Development Curriculum — V1.0**

No more restructuring for now.

I'd give V1 a reasonable lifespan — perhaps **3–6 months** — before doing a V1.1 review. During that period, the board should change because you're **completing cards**, not because you're continually reconsidering the curriculum.

And I'd keep the rule we established earlier:

> **Three cards in NOW. Finish one before promoting another.**

That single constraint is probably more valuable than any individual book, course or technology we've put on the board.

You've now got something considerably better than a giant list of things software developers are supposedly meant to know. You've got a manageable curriculum built around **Java/Spring depth, backend/software-engineering breadth, architecture, production engineering, AI integration and actual building**.

**V1.0: done. Time to study.**
